rationale: The nesting does deliver the claimed equal 25% weights and the four legs are economically distinct, but this is largely an ensemble-stacking extension of the archived gen-6 composite (gap+vol+trough, alpha −0.059/t −4.55) with one extra leg, so the expected gain is incremental and dilution of the strongest leg (downside asymmetry, alpha −0.067) is a real risk.

This is a single-leg substitution (trough coverage → margin downside asymmetry) inside the already-tested FundingGapWithInstabilityAndTroughCoverage structure with identical 50/25/25 weights, making it a cosmetic variant whose only differentiator from Proposal 1 is leg weighting rather than a new mechanism.

Swapping pretax-margin asymmetry for gross-margin asymmetry is a defensible operating-vs-below-the-line attribution test and the sign logic is internally consistent, but it remains a one-variable perturbation of the archive's best signal and the archive already shows gross-margin-based legs (MarginErosionUnderThinCash, ShortTermFundedAssetsThinMargin) behave similarly, limiting the informational payoff.

The change in short-term debt share as a creditor-revealed distress footprint is a genuinely new channel relative to the archive's static maturity-share test, the partner leg avoids the (dlc−che)/act crowding that saturates the rest of the archive, and the sign is coherent — the main risks are denominator instability for near-zero-debt firms and noise in a one-year delta.

The tail-of-the-burn-distribution construction is internally consistent (TS_MIN picks the worst drawdown, NEG orients it toward distress) and generalizes the working downside-tail principle to the cash process, though it partly re-uses che on both legs and is close in spirit to the already-tested CashBurnWithNearTermClaims.

A legitimate attribution test with correct sign orientation, but the decomposition is incomplete — it substitutes only the cash component of (dlc−che)/act while never testing dlc/act alone, so a null result cannot cleanly separate "cash scarcity" from "rollover debt," and −che/act is itself close to the published cash-holdings characteristic.
